title: BrewBooze: Barista and Bartender Drinks Simulator Integrated with Business Cost Prediction Using Multiple Linear Regression
authors: Lexter Louis T. Apuada, Marilou B. Mangrobang, Rimuel S. Cañada, M. A. Mercado, C. Centeno, A. A. C. Sison
abstract: This research aimed to develop an innovative system that simulates the creation of barista and bartender beverages, enhances customer satisfaction through personalized coffee and cocktail flavor recommendations, and predicts startup costs for cafés. The system uses 3D models to guide users through beverage-making processes, and the GPT OpenAI API powers its flavor recommendation engine for accuracy and personalization. Additionally, multiple linear regression was employed to provide entrepreneurs with a detailed cost breakdown based on their capital and the year of establishment. BrewBooze was evaluated through a survey using Google Forms, having IT professionals, baristas, bartenders, and general consumers as their respondents. Half of the respondents drink their coffee/cocktail more than three times a week and only a quarter of them do not know the process of making it. Results have also shown that people are satisfied with the coffee/cocktail they are ordering and for the entrepreneurial side, most respondents prefer to have a capital of less than a million pesos, making it insufficient for starting a café. The ISO 25010 software quality model assessed the system, focusing on functional suitability, reliability, performance efficiency, and usability. The results returned a very satisfactory score, indicating that BrewBooze effectively simulates beverages, provides accurate flavor recommendations, and predicts startup costs, making it a valuable tool for both consumers and aspiring café owners.

title: Evaluating Personality Traits in Large Language Models: Insights from Psychological Questionnaires
authors: Bhandari, Pranav; Naseem, Usman; Datta, Amitava; Fay, Nicolas; Nasim, Mehwish
abstract: Psychological assessment tools have long helped humans understand behavioural patterns. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate content comparable to that of humans, we explore whether they exhibit personality traits. To this end, this work applies psychological tools to LLMs in diverse scenarios to generate personality profiles. Using established trait-based questionnaires such as the Big Five Inventory and by addressing the possibility of training data contamination, we examine the dimensional variability and dominance of LLMs across five core personality dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. Our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit unique dominant traits, varying characteristics, and distinct personality profiles even within the same family of models.

title: Using Large Language Models to Tackle Fundamental Challenges in Graph Learning: A Comprehensive Survey
authors: Mengran Li, Pengyu Zhang, Wenbin Xing, Yijia Zheng, Klim Zaporojets, Junzhou Chen, Ronghui Zhang, Yong Zhang, Siyuan Gong, Jia Hu, Xiaolei Ma, Zhiyuan Liu, Paul Groth, Marcel Worring

title: Insight Through Dialogue: A Practical Exploration of AIGC in Cross-cultural Design Research
authors: Zhao, Xiaoxuan; Qiu, Yue
abstract: This study systematically reviews the objectives, methodologies, and challenges involved in cross-cultural design research, analyzing the benefits of employing Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content (AIGC) for such studies. It introduces a novel tool that applies AIGC to cross-cultural design research, developed through the use of a fine-tuned ChatGPT-4 model. By creating a specific dataset for the research topic and applying transfer learning techniques, this tool evolves into a chatbot capable of delivering personalized response strategies to users from diverse cultural backgrounds. It leverages natural language interfaces and real-time image generation to meet user needs, conducting research tasks autonomously. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with conventional cross-cultural research methods such as questionnaires and manual interviews, the chatbot significantly enhances the efficiency of design research and users' cross-cultural interaction experience, while obtaining more realistic and objective feedback. This study not only underscores the potential application of AIGC in cross-cultural design research but also provides substantial theoretical support and practical guidance for future research in cross-cultural contexts.

title: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Minimal Effort
authors: Zhenyu Wu, Qingkai Zeng, Zhihan Zhang, Zhaoxuan Tan, Chao Shen, Meng Jiang
